# Plants, fungi and the rest of the eukaryotes

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft

Written from `research/03-plants-fungi-other.yml` and not yet reviewed by a
second reader.

Two limits run through it. Thirty-one of its sources were read as abstracts
rather than as full text, which is the second-largest such count in the book,
and much of the plant work on flowering time predates full-text indexing. The
apicomplexan material also leans on one laboratory, and @sec-protists says so
where it matters.
:::

Two kinds of statement get made about isoforms outside the animals. One is a
percentage, saying that some fraction of some organism's genes is alternatively
spliced. The other names a gene, changes which isoform the organism can make,
and reports what happened to the organism. They are not equally secure, and this
chapter leans on the second kind. Where it gives a percentage it says which
assay produced the number.

The reason to distrust the percentages was stated by the people who first tried
the comparison. Detected splicing scales with how deeply a transcriptome has
been sampled. Library construction and sequence quality differ between projects.
Those authors therefore concluded that it was impractical to state the exact
level of alternative splicing even in the organisms they had tested themselves
[@kim2006eukaryotes]. Their cleanest demonstration is a pair of rodents. Mouse
and rat separated around 23 million years ago. The mouse transcriptome was much
the better sampled of the two, and it yielded significantly more alternative
splicing, a gap that tracks sequencing effort rather than biology
[@kim2006eukaryotes].

Their fix for it is crude and deliberate. Keep only genes with at least ten
sequenced transcripts, draw ten of those at random, and count the splicing
events in that sample, then repeat a hundred times and average the result
[@kim2006eukaryotes]. After that treatment the two rodents come out alike. A
fungal survey later measured how much work the correction does. Across its
species the raw count of detected events tracked the number of available
transcript sequences at a correlation of 0.82. Expressed instead as a per-gene
rate from fixed-size random samples, the same dependence fell to 0.16 and lost
significance [@grutzmann2013fungal]. Those authors capped their own sampling at
ten transcripts per locus, because the chance of finding an alternative event
keeps rising with depth while the gain per added transcript shrinks
[@grutzmann2013fungal].

The unit of counting moves the answer too. Scoring a gene as spliced or not is a
different measurement from counting events per gene, and the gap between them
widens across lineages. By one uniform index *Plasmodium falciparum* has 3 per
cent of its well-sampled genes spliced, at an average of 0.09 events per gene.
Human has 88 per cent and 5.35 events [@chen2014complexity]. That is a
thirtyfold difference on the first measure and roughly sixtyfold on the second.

What survives all of this is the comparison made inside one study by one method.
The broadest such comparison covers 1,494 species. It reports splicing as
minimal in prokaryotes and single-celled eukaryotes, highest in mammals and
birds, and no more than moderate in plants, despite wide variation in plant
genome composition [@delafuente2025treeoflife]. Three features of it matter for
the rest of this chapter. Its metric is an annotation statistic rather than a
transcript measurement: the summed length of every annotated coding sequence,
divided by the footprint of those sequences on the genome, which rises when the
same DNA is reused across several annotated isoforms
[@delafuente2025treeoflife]. More than half the headline species count is
prokaryotic and was sampled rather than surveyed, since annotations were
available for 694 eukaryotes and 400 archaeal and 400 bacterial genomes were
added at random [@delafuente2025treeoflife].

The third feature is a limit that falls precisely on the organisms of this
chapter. Fungal and single-celled eukaryotic genomes in that reference set are
not annotated through the RNA-seq-driven pipeline, and carry few or no
alternative isoforms on record. Those authors say plainly that the absence of
annotation is not evidence that the organisms do not splice
[@delafuente2025treeoflife]. Their own audit found one significant bias, and it
points upward: better-evidenced annotation yields higher splicing estimates, so
a normalised figure is reported beside the raw one
[@delafuente2025treeoflife]. One relationship in the same work is not a
confounder at all. Splicing is highest neither in the most gene-dense genomes
nor in the most spacious, but in those where about half the sequence is
intergenic, and plant genomes have pushed well past that point without gaining
isoforms for it [@delafuente2025treeoflife].

## Plants {#sec-plants}

A normalised deep-coverage survey of Arabidopsis put alternative splicing at
61.2 per cent of intron-containing genes, in flower and seedling tissue grown
without stress, and those authors treat the figure as a floor
[@marquez2012arabidopsis]. It is worth knowing what produced it. Total RNA from
Col-0 flowers and ten-day-old seedlings was mixed in equal parts, normalised to
flatten the abundance distribution, and read as roughly 116 million paired
75-base reads [@marquez2012arabidopsis]. Change only the counting rule on that
one dataset and the figure moves ten points. Splicing scored from overlapping
introns, a rule blind to retained introns, gives about 52 per cent of the same
genes in the same sample [@marquez2012arabidopsis].

Published plant figures climbed from about one per cent to over thirty across
six estimates between 2003 and 2006. The authors who tabulated that climb
attribute it to growing transcript coverage rather than to any revision of the
biology [@marquez2012arabidopsis]. A looser figure of 60 to 70 per cent of
intron-containing genes also circulates, with no species, tissue, condition or
depth attached, sourced to a review rather than to a measurement
[@betz2024mycorrhizal]. The contrast most often quoted sets roughly 70 per cent
of multi-exon plant genes against over 95 per cent in animals. It reaches
readers as one introductory sentence backed by three references jointly, with no
indication of which reference carries which number
[@reyes2026arabidopsisproteome].

Mass spectrometry has begun to put plant isoforms on the protein side of the
ledger. A search of Arabidopsis proteomes against the Araport11 gene models
yielded 471,196 peptides from 22,479 proteins. Of those, 32,110 were specific to
a single isoform, and they resolved into 2,442 distinct splicing events, 879 of
them retained introns [@reyes2026arabidopsisproteome]. The scale is an
aggregation rather than one experiment, pooling over 900 mass spectrometry
datasets, 720 of them taken from public repositories
[@reyes2026arabidopsisproteome].

### Intron retention is the commonest event {#sec-class-balance}

The flavour differs as much as the amount. Cassette exons predominate in
animals, while intron retention is the more frequent class in other taxa
[@grutzmann2013fungal]. The five event names are defined in @sec-event-classes.
Arabidopsis follows the second pattern, with intron retention the single
commonest event class in that survey, at roughly two fifths of everything the
transcript assembly detected [@marquez2012arabidopsis].

Two qualifications come from the people who state the pattern. One is
quantitative: most retained introns in that survey were supported by far fewer
reads than the junction that removes them, and about 73 per cent had a retention
ratio below 1 [@marquez2012arabidopsis]. Counting events therefore overstates
how much retained-intron RNA a plant cell is actually holding. The other
qualification is that which mode comes out on top depends on the tissues sampled
and on how the plants were grown [@li2021maize]. That makes the plant-against-mammal
contrast a statement about an experiment as well as about a kingdom.

### Flowering time and the problem of dose

Flowering in Arabidopsis is set partly by how two genes are spliced, and FLM is
the better known of them. Its transcripts were cloned and sequenced at three
growth temperatures. The share of non-canonical isoforms, which mostly carry
premature stop codons, rose from 30 per cent at 16 degrees to over 50 per cent
at 27 degrees [@capovilla2017flm]. Two isoforms dominate, FLM-beta and
FLM-delta, and what the warm one does has been argued over for more than a
decade.

The original account was antagonism between the two. Both isoforms were reported
to compete for the same partner, SHORT VEGETATIVE PHASE. The beta-containing
complex forms mainly in the cold and holds flowering back
[@flm2013antagonisticvariants]. The complex formed with FLM-delta was described
as unable to bind DNA, and as acting dominant-negatively to promote flowering as
temperature rises [@flm2013antagonisticvariants]. A second report the same year
described the system by abundance instead, attributing the repression of
flowering to the accumulation of FLM-beta as temperature falls
[@flm2013madsboxrepressors]. The same authors found that *svp* and *flm* mutants
each lose temperature responsiveness over different temperature ranges
[@flm2013madsboxrepressors]. That places the two genes at different points of
the scale rather than in one switch.

Then the dominant-negative model lost its necessity. A later report proposed
that warmth does not create an inhibitor at all but destroys the repressor. High
temperature shifts FLM splicing toward transcripts cleared by nonsense-mediated
decay, so the functional isoform simply runs out [@flm2016asnmd]. Those authors
identified individual temperature-sensitive splice sites in the gene. They
concluded that the rise in decay-targeted transcripts accounts for most of the
temperature effect, rather than any change in the ratio of two coding forms
[@flm2016asnmd]. The mechanism of unproductive splicing is described in
@sec-as-nmd.

The experiment that ought to settle it instead split in two. CRISPR deletion of
FLM exon 2 at the endogenous locus leaves the plant making FLM-delta and no
FLM-beta. Those plants flowered earlier than wild type, but never earlier than a
complete FLM null, which is not the ordering a dominant-negative isoform would
produce [@capovilla2017flm]. The same paper drove the FLM-delta reading
frame from a constitutive promoter in a null background. Those plants did flower
significantly earlier than controls at 16 degrees, which the authors read as
confirming the dominant-negative model once the isoform is present at high dose
[@capovilla2017flm]. Both results come from one laboratory and one figure set.
The honest summary is that FLM-delta can act as an inhibitor at a dose the plant
never reaches.

Two further lines of evidence sit on either side. One argues against a ratio at
all. Comparing flowering time against isoform levels across three independent
experiments, FLM-beta abundance tracked flowering far better than FLM-delta did,
most sharply at 15 degrees, and those authors concluded that the level of
FLM-beta alone sets flowering time [@lutz2015flmnatural]. The other gives
FLM-delta work other than DNA binding. It accelerated degradation of the SVP
protein at high temperature, apparently through ubiquitination, faster than
FLM-beta did [@flm2022svpstability]. The two isoforms also meet their shared
partner in different compartments. FLM-beta carries SVP into the nucleus in the
cold, while SVP met FLM-delta mainly in the cytoplasm when warm
[@flm2022svpstability].

### Natural alleles that move the same ratio

Wild accessions supply the perturbations a laboratory would struggle to design.
Early flowering in the Killean-0 accession traces to a 5.7 kb retroelement in
the first intron of FLM. Engineering that insertion out of the Kil-0 allele
restored late flowering, and engineering the same element into the Columbia
allele reproduced both the drop in FLM expression and the change in its splicing
[@lutz2015flmnatural]. The insertion does not change how often transcription
starts. Pre-mRNA upstream of it was unchanged while pre-mRNA downstream fell,
and the locus instead made polyadenylated intron-1 transcripts carrying a
premature stop, which cycloheximide stabilised [@lutz2015flmnatural]. So the
full-length message is lost to premature termination, aberrant splicing and
decay rather than to a quieter promoter.

A panel of unrelated insertions of similar size placed in the same intron
reproduced the effect, and those landing further along it cut FLM-delta
particularly hard. All four lines scored for flowering flowered earlier than
their wild type, whatever their FLM-delta level [@lutz2015flmnatural]. That is
the ratio model's hardest result to accommodate.

One base is enough in another accession. In Can-0, from the Canary Islands, a
single substitution in FLM intron 2 creates a new splice acceptor that
outcompetes the native one, adding 17 nucleotides and a premature stop to almost
every transcript. Putting that one substitution into an otherwise Columbia FLM
construct destroyed its ability to rescue the *flm-3* mutant
[@hanemian2020flmpleiotropy].

### MAF2 arrives at the same trick, and two labs disagree about it

MAF2 acquired temperature-dependent splicing independently of FLM. At low
temperature its abundant variant encodes a protein that partners SVP to
repress flowering. Warming shifts the balance toward an intron-retaining variant
carrying a premature stop, whose product can neither bind SVP nor repress
[@airoldi2015maf2]. Yeast two-hybrid tests separated the isoforms by partner
binding. Three of four bound full-length SVP, while the warm-abundant variant,
missing part of its K domain, showed no detectable interaction
[@airoldi2015maf2]. Knocking out MAF2 and FLM together gave a far more severe
early-flowering phenotype at 16 degrees than either alone [@airoldi2015maf2]. Two
genes of one clade that separately acquired thermosensory splicing therefore act
by separate and additive routes.

One detail of that case corrects an assumption worth naming. The warm variant
carries a premature stop codon, which invites the conclusion that warmth works
by decay. That variant's level did not rise in *upf1*, *upf3* or *smg7* mutants, so it is
not a decay substrate at all [@airoldi2015maf2]. Warming works here by
subtracting the active isoform rather than by destroying anything. A rare third variant behaved
like the model's FLM-delta when overexpressed, promoting flowering rather than
delaying it, and the same paper found it barely expressed at any temperature
[@airoldi2015maf2]. The dose objection to the FLM case thus reappears in a
second gene.

An earlier study of MAF2 reached the opposite conclusion from the same kind of
experiment. Overexpressing the genomic clone delayed flowering, but no
individual splice variant did, and the cold-abundant variant instead made plants
flower pronouncedly early in two backgrounds
[@rosloski2012maf2variants]. Those authors repeated the test in an accession
null for FLC and MAF2 expression, which also fails to express MAF3 and MAF4
properly, so that co-suppression of relatives could not confound the result. The
genomic clone still delayed flowering while the cold-abundant variant alone did
not under long days, although under short days it gave the same spread of
flowering times as the clone [@rosloski2012maf2variants]. Photoperiod does not
reconcile the two studies, since both scored long days. What differs is
background and transgene integrity, and the disagreement is unresolved.

### COOLAIR, and whether the antisense isoforms are needed at all

Vernalisation at the FLC locus runs partly through isoform choice on the
antisense strand. The cold-induced COOLAIR transcripts exist as several isoforms
distinguished by splicing and polyadenylation, and the cold-specific distal
class II.ii isoform represses FLC by sequestering the activator FRIGIDA away
from the FLC promoter [@long2024coolair]. The proximal polyadenylation choice is
actively directed rather than incidental. Two conserved 3'-end processing
factors were required to process the antisense transcripts but not the sense
ones. An RNA-binding protein steered them to the proximal site, and that
targeted processing reduced sense transcription
[@coolair2010targetedprocessing].

Single-base experiments make the isoform choice causal. Changing one base so
that a COOLAIR splice acceptor read AA instead of AG reduced that intron's
splicing and the use of the proximal poly(A) site, and raised FLC expression
[@marquardt2014coolair]. A natural polymorphism beside a COOLAIR splice acceptor
does the same thing in both directions. Introducing it into the Columbia allele
added an exon to COOLAIR, and reverting it in the variant allele restored the
Columbia pattern, with FLC sense splicing unchanged throughout
[@li2015coolairsplicing]. Lines carrying the late allele expressed FLC more
highly before, during and after cold, and flowered considerably later after four
weeks of vernalisation [@li2015coolairsplicing]. The step joining antisense
splicing to sense output appears to be capping, since the late allele's FLC
transcripts carried a 5' cap more often and the single base change reproduced
that shift [@li2015coolairsplicing].

The control that matters most for interpreting all this is the one that removes
COOLAIR first. When the same polymorphism was placed in an FLC allele whose
COOLAIR promoter had been replaced, so that no antisense transcript was made, it
changed neither FLC expression nor flowering time
[@li2015coolairsplicing]. That puts the effect of the base change inside COOLAIR
rather than beside it.

Whether COOLAIR is needed for vernalisation at all is a different question, and
the literature answers it both ways. T-DNA insertions that removed the distal
COOLAIR transcripts, or both the distal and the proximal ones, left FLC stably
repressed by cold, with histone marks tracking the wild-type allele
[@helliwell2011coolairnot]. Small CRISPR deletions in the COOLAIR promoter that
left the rest of the locus intact abolished detectable COOLAIR and still let
vernalisation accelerate flowering as in wild type
[@jeon2023coolaircbf]. In those same mutants FLC was silenced by prolonged cold
as in wild type [@jeon2023coolaircbf].

One result rescues the requirement, under conditions closer to a field.
Following a freezing night, wild-type FLC drops sharply, and that drop did not
happen in lines where COOLAIR had been truncated; forcing COOLAIR high lowered
FLC, and the COOLAIR knockout suppressed that effect
[@zhao2021coolairfield]. The same group then raised an objection that applies to
every negative result above. Every allele they examined that was built to remove
COOLAIR, the terminator-exchange transgenes and a CRISPR promoter deletion
alike, turned out to make new antisense transcripts starting inside the first
intron of FLC [@zhao2021coolairfield]. If removing COOLAIR replaces it with
something, a null result is hard to read.

The authors of one negative result tested that objection directly. Wild type makes low-abundance convergent antisense transcripts at the locus as
well. Cold reduced those to the same extent in wild type and in every deletion
mutant, so their regulation does not depend on COOLAIR
[@jeon2023coolaircbf]. A later study supplies the most likely reconciliation.
The Polycomb route can silence FLC on its own. In COOLAIR-defective lines the
active mark was removed more slowly during cold, and the locus still ended up
fully silenced, whether the antisense pathway was crippled or driven hard
[@nielsen2024coolairprc2]. Two parallel routes to one outcome would explain why
the requirement appears and disappears with growth conditions.

### The clock splices itself unproductively

A systematic survey of Arabidopsis clock genes found unproductive splicing
widespread among them, mostly full or partial intron retention generating
in-frame premature stops. The CCA1 and LHY variants are conserved between the
two paralogues, and the CCA1 event is conserved across plant phyla
[@filichkin2012clock]. A system-wide survey under temperature change separated
splicing from transcription for one gene, finding the LHY transcript falling on
cooling while LHY promoter strength did not change
[@clock2012astemperature]. Barley seedlings shifted to low temperature change
the splicing of core clock genes including the orthologues of LHY and PRR7,
which puts the mechanism in a monocot crop as well [@calixto2016barley].

One clock variant has been tested as an isoform rather than as a transcript.
Overexpressing an alternatively spliced CCA1 variant shortened the circadian
period, as deleting both CCA1 and LHY does. The variant was reported to pair
with the functional proteins into heterodimers that bind DNA poorly
[@cca12012selfregulatory]. The same variant moved a whole-plant phenotype.
Plants overexpressing the full-length form tolerated freezing better, those
overexpressing the variant were freezing-sensitive, and cold suppressed
production of the variant [@cca12012selfregulatory]. A later study bounds the
case on dose, reporting that at normal growth temperature the variant protein
could be detected only after immunoprecipitation enrichment, and that raising
its level took 37 degrees [@cca12021proteinvariants].

The tightest clock result addresses the switch itself. REVEILLE2 has an
alternative exon whose inclusion switches on cooling, and a T-DNA insertion
landing inside that exon removed the cold induction of the productive
full-length transcript [@james2024rve2]. That allele lengthened the circadian
period by about 0.32 hours at 20 degrees and about 1.1 hours after chilling to
12 degrees [@james2024rve2]. The effect grows in exactly the condition where
the isoform switch happens. It also changed clock output at isoform
resolution, altering specific transcript isoforms of RVE6, PRR5 and ELF4
[@james2024rve2]. The PRR5 isoform acquired a second peak after cooling that
wild type does not have [@james2024rve2]. Those three results were read from
the preprint rather than from the published version.

### Resistance genes need their introns, except when they do not

The largest body of functional evidence in plant isoform biology sits in
disease resistance, and it does not resolve into a rule. Four genes have been
tested by the same logic, and three of the answers disagree with the fourth.

Tobacco *N* confers resistance to tobacco mosaic virus, and its transcripts
include a shorter form that encodes a truncated receptor. A transgene built from
cDNA can make the complete receptor but not the short one, and plants carrying
it fell short of complete resistance. Restoring the alternative exon's intron to
the same transgene restored both transcripts and full resistance
[@ngene2000alttranscripts]. The two transcripts are not made in fixed
proportion. The one coding the full receptor dominates before infection and for
the first three hours after it, and the truncated form becomes the more abundant
from four to eight hours [@ngene2000alttranscripts]. That is the timescale of
the defence response itself. *N*-mediated resistance also fails at 30 degrees,
and the failure is visible in the transcripts, since both forms accumulated in
inoculated leaves at the permissive 20 degrees and neither did at 30
[@ngene2006transcriptaccumulation]. The cell death that *N* triggers looks like
a threshold rather than a graded response, with transcripts of both forms rising
to substantial levels just before cells died
[@ngene2006transcriptaccumulation].

Arabidopsis *RPS4* carries the same requirement with cleaner controls.
Deleting either or both of its two retained introns from a working transgene
destroyed resistance and left the gene's expression level untouched
[@rps42003truncatedorfs]. That rules out the obvious alternative, which is
that the introns are simply there to make the gene express well. What the
truncated product does was also tested rather than assumed. The truncated
transgene alone gave no resistance. Supplying the intron-less and the
truncated transgenes together in one plant restored partial resistance, which
those authors read as the short transcript working through its protein rather
than as a regulatory RNA [@rps42003truncatedorfs]. A later study closed the
remaining loophole. When single introns were deleted, the splicing frequency
of the introns that remained was measured and did not change, so the loss of
function cannot be blamed on disturbed splicing elsewhere in the gene
[@rps42007inducedsplicing]. The truncated proteins are not inert either.
Expressed transiently in *Nicotiana benthamiana* they set off cell death
resembling the hypersensitive response with no effector present, and the
different truncated forms differed markedly in stability
[@rps42007inducedsplicing]. A legume supplies the third positive case. *RCT1*
of *Medicago truncatula* confers anthracnose resistance and retains intron 4
to make a protein lacking only its C-terminal tail, and neither the regular
nor the intron-retaining transcript alone was enough for resistance
[@rct12013splicingrequired].

Then the pattern breaks, in a gene of the same family. Flax *L6* makes four
transcript classes by splicing its third intron, three of them coding
truncated products. Put into flax as an intronless transgene that cannot make
any of them, the gene conferred rust resistance indistinguishable from the
wild-type allele [@l61999alternativetranscripts]. There is also nothing for an
infection-induced switch to explain in that gene. Its four transcript classes
are present in every organ examined, and expression was not induced when
resistant plants met an avirulent rust carrying the matching avirulence gene
[@l61999alternativetranscripts]. Tomato *Bs4* joins flax on the negative side.
Those transcripts retain an intron, and a derivative with the introns removed
still detected the *Xanthomonas* effector AvrBs4, which the authors read as
the splice variants not being crucial [@bs42004tirnblrr]. The same gene
nonetheless supplies a natural splicing variant with a consequence. The
susceptible allele of a wild tomato relative is more than 98 per cent
identical to the functional gene and shares its exon-intron structure. The two
differ by a splice polymorphism in intron 2 that truncates the predicted
protein [@bs42004tirnblrr].

Rice gives a third kind of answer. The blast resistance gene *RGA5* makes two
transcripts, and genetic tests put the resistance entirely with the first of
them, the second having no detectable activity [@rga52013directbinding].
Alternative splicing there produces a spare rather than a partner. The reason
is a domain outside the leucine-rich repeats. The effector-binding region sits
in the C terminus of the active isoform, resembles the recognition domain of
another rice resistance protein, and binds two blast effectors directly
[@rga52013directbinding].

One more result unsettles the clearest positive case, and it comes from the
tobacco gene. A study set out to separate intron effects from splicing
effects. The boost in transcript level tracks introns 1 and 2 rather than the
intron carrying the alternative exon. A transgene whose alternative-exon
splice sites had been mutated away still accumulated transcript as well as the
fully introned gene [@ikeda2021nintrons]. The same study then contradicted the
requirement itself. A transgene carrying introns 1 and 2, but not the intron
holding the alternative exon, developed full chalky white necrosis as fast as
the construct with all four introns. It restricted virus spread in *N.
benthamiana* as well [@ikeda2021nintrons]. The two experiments are not a clean
head-to-head. The 2000 work used stable tobacco transgenics in the gene's own
context. The 2021 work used transient constructs driven by a strong viral
promoter in a different host. Which assay to believe is exactly the question a
reader is left with.

A last caution applies to all of these cases. *RPS4*'s splicing pattern does
change during the resistance response, and its expression is induced by the
effector in a way that requires EDS1. The same study found inducible splicing
changes outside that gene-for-gene pairing
[@rps42007inducedsplicing]. An induced isoform shift is therefore not by itself
evidence that the shift is doing the resisting.

Splicing regulators reach these genes from outside. Losing the receptor that
imports SR proteins into the nucleus changes the transcript mixture of two
named resistance genes and costs the plant resistance. In the Arabidopsis
*mos14-1* mutant the two *RPS4* variants that each retain one intron rose,
while the normally spliced transcript fell. That mutant supported about ten
times as much *Pseudomonas syringae* carrying the matching effector
[@xu2011mos14]. Splicing of actin and beta-tubulin was unchanged in that
mutant, so the failure is not splicing-wide [@xu2011mos14]. The levels of both
resistance-gene transcripts fell as well as shifting in proportion, so the
effect is not purely a change of mixture either. The related autoimmune *snc1*
allele needs its own introns to misbehave, since transgenic plants given the
mutant coding sequence as cDNA never developed the dwarf stature the
intron-containing allele causes [@xu2011mos14].

### One isoform, at its own expression level

Three plant cases use a tighter design than the intron deletions above. Each
supplies one isoform at close to native expression and then watches a whole
plant. That design is worth naming, because it is what the resistance-gene
literature has mostly lacked.

The first is a brake on immune signalling. Losing the RNA-binding protein IRR
raised the share of the intron-retaining *CPK28* transcript sixfold relative
to total *CPK28* [@dressano2020irr]. Infection raised that same share in
wild-type plants, so the shift is part of the normal response. The two
transcripts were then put back separately from the same promoter. The normally
spliced form restored ordinary bacterial growth in the mutant, and the
intron-retaining form left the plants as over-resistant as the mutant itself
[@dressano2020irr]. The retained intron removes the part of the kinase that
senses calcium, which is why the short protein functions poorly as a negative
regulator rather than not at all [@dressano2020irr].

The second divides the jobs of a splicing factor between its own two isoforms.
In an Arabidopsis mutant lacking both SR45 isoforms, the first restored normal
flower petals but not root growth, and the second restored root growth but not
petal shape [@sr452009distinctisoforms]. What distinguishes them is a
phosphorylation site inside the alternatively spliced segment. Mutating
serine-219 on its own left the complementation pattern unchanged
[@sr452009distinctisoforms]. Mutating it together with the adjacent
threonine-218 made the first isoform behave like the second, complementing
root growth and not petal shape [@sr452009distinctisoforms]. Defence separates
the two isoforms as well. Plants lacking SR45 are over-immune, and lines
expressing only the first isoform brought the exaggerated response back to
wild type against three *Pseudomonas* strains and an oomycete, while lines
expressing only the second did not [@bui2025sr45immunity]. One of that
regulator's targets is a receptor gene whose own isoform ratio reverses.
Retention of the first intron of *CBRLK1* removes its kinase domain, and the
kinase-less form dominates in the SR45 null. Overexpressing it in wild-type
plants produced resistance partway to the null, while the full-length form did
nothing [@bui2025sr45immunity]. A second target runs the other way, and shows
how much of this remains inference. *SRF1*'s full-length form is the one that
rises in the null, and overexpressing it again gave immunity partway to the
null. The truncated form could not be tested at all, because it was too scarce
to clone [@bui2025sr45immunity].

The third is a hormone repressor that escapes destruction. JAZ10.4 lacks the
Jas domain through which the jasmonate receptor marks these repressors for
degradation, is accordingly resistant to hormone-induced destruction, and
makes plants strongly insensitive to jasmonate when overexpressed
[@jaz102009tifymotif]. It also works at its own gene's expression level.
Expressed from the native *JAZ10* promoter it rescued the
hormone-hypersensitive phenotype of a *jaz10* mutant, and jasmonate treatment
made the variant protein accumulate quickly [@jaz102013negativefeedback]. The
variant keeps a route to its targets after losing the canonical one. A cryptic
MYC2-binding site at its N-terminal end, and a ZIM motif acting as a
transferable repressor domain, recruit the corepressor NINJA
[@jaz102013negativefeedback]. Strongly expressing a *JAZ10* genomic clone that
still contains the intron was enough to repress jasmonate responses, so the
plant's own splicing machinery makes enough of the repressive form from an
unmodified gene [@jaz2010dominantrepressors].

The group that found the first of these variants also published the result that
keeps the family honest. Across the Arabidopsis JAZ family, variants retaining a
conserved intron that splits the receptor-binding motif bind the receptor less
well, and when the cDNAs were overexpressed only some of them repressed
signalling [@jaz2010dominantrepressors]. Not every truncated splice variant does
something, on the evidence of the people best placed to claim otherwise.

### An ABA phosphatase that works both ways

Abscisic acid signalling has the clearest opposing-isoform pair in plants.
HAB1.1 and HAB1.2 are products of alternative splicing of one phosphatase
gene. They were reported to play opposing roles in ABA-controlled seed
germination and in the growth arrest that follows it, with the second made
mainly when ABA is present [@hab12015antagonisticvariants]. The mechanism is a
separation of binding from catalysis. HAB1.2 still interacts with the kinase
OST1 that the normal phosphatase switches off, and cannot inhibit that
kinase's activity, which turns a negative regulator of ABA signalling into a
positive one [@hab12015antagonisticvariants].

Three unrelated lesions then converge on the same splice choice, which is the
strongest argument that the choice is load-bearing. Arabidopsis mutants lacking
the spliceosomal Sm core protein SmEb are hypersensitive to ABA and make less
HAB1.1 and more HAB1.2; overexpressing HAB1.1 rescued them and overexpressing
HAB1.2 did not [@hong2021smeb]. Mutants lacking three SR-protein kinases of the
SRPKII family are hypersensitive during seedling establishment, those kinases
normally favour HAB1.1, and overexpressing HAB1.1 restored ordinary sensitivity
[@hab12026srpkii]. A forward-genetic screen for over-sensitivity to ABA landed
on the RNA-binding protein RBM25, whose mutants mis-splice *HAB1* badly, and
supplying a *HAB1* copy built from wild-type messages partly undid the phenotype
[@rbm252015pwirrm]. The kinases act through a named intermediate, since they
phosphorylate the SR-like protein SR45 and that phosphorylation is what shifts
*HAB1* splicing [@hab12026srpkii].

### Splice alleles that a breeding programme would take

Four crop loci show the effect sizes involved, and they are not large. In
tropical japonica rice, six SNPs at the OsLG3b locus change how the OsMADS1
transcript is spliced, and that splice variation was associated with grain
length in a candidate-region analysis [@yu2018oslg3b]. A near-isogenic line
carried the large-grain donor allele in a Nipponbare background. Its grains
were 7.5 per cent longer and 3.5 per cent thicker, and yield per plant rose
7.1 per cent [@yu2018oslg3b]. Heading date, tiller number and grains per
panicle did not change significantly [@yu2018oslg3b].

Bread wheat makes five splice variants of the G-protein gamma subunit gene
TaGS3, and two of them pull in opposite directions. Overexpressing TaGS3.1 cut
grain weight by 5.89 per cent and length by 5.04 per cent. Overexpressing
TaGS3.5 raised grain weight by 5.70 per cent and length by 4.30 per cent
[@ren2021tags3]. A second wheat locus makes the same point with a natural
allele instead of a transgene, and at two ploidies. A G-to-A change at the
splice acceptor of TaGW2-A1 exon 5 mis-splices the transcript. Backcrossed
tetraploid and hexaploid lines carrying it gained 6.6 per cent in grain
weight, 2.8 per cent in width and 2.1 per cent in length across thirteen
experiments [@simmonds2016tagw2]. One broken splice site can make two
products, which is worth remembering before treating such an allele as a
knockout. Nine of twelve sequenced cDNA clones used an acceptor four bases
downstream, giving a frameshift and a 134-residue truncated protein. Three
used one nine bases downstream, giving a nearly normal protein missing three
conserved residues [@simmonds2016tagw2].

The oldest of these traits is rice grain quality, and it rests on a single
letter at a splice site. The two common Waxy alleles differ by a GT against a
TT at the donor site of intron 1, and that difference changes how efficiently
the intron is spliced. The two alleles separate rice into the
intermediate-to-high and the low-to-intermediate amylose classes
[@liu2022waxyintron]. Cutting the intron out moved the trait. CRISPR deletion
of the first intron raised grain amylose from 13 per cent to about 24 per cent
in two lines carrying the poorly spliced allele. It did nothing measurable in
lines carrying the efficiently spliced one [@liu2022waxyintron]. That second
half is the control which makes the splicing interpretation stick. A rice
splicing regulator has since been traced to the same target. A mutation in a
C2H2 zinc-finger gene lowered grain amylose by specifically reducing the
splicing efficiency of intron 1 in the Waxy-b allele [@sakaguchi2025lowac2].
Crossing that mutant to the efficiently spliced Waxy-a allele left the
allele's splicing normal, while the Waxy-b first intron was still affected
[@sakaguchi2025lowac2]. The regulator acts on one allele of one gene rather
than on splicing in general.

Two further cases sit at the level of flowering rather than grain. In the
temperate grass *Brachypodium distachyon* the florigen gene FT2 makes a
second, shorter isoform, and overexpressing just that isoform delayed bolting
by six to twelve days [@qin2017ft2splicing]. The reciprocal test went the
other way. Knocking down only the short isoform, with an artificial microRNA
aimed at its isoform-specific sequence, advanced heading by about eight days
[@qin2017ft2splicing]. The matching reagent against the full-length isoform
delayed heading severely [@qin2017ft2splicing]. The short isoform also has the
properties a competitive repressor needs. Across yeast two-hybrid,
split-fluorophore and co-immunoprecipitation assays it bound neither the bZIP
partner nor any 14-3-3 protein that the full-length protein binds
[@qin2017ft2splicing]. It still heterodimerised with the full-length protein
and with the second florigen [@qin2017ft2splicing]. Tomato's master ripening
transcription factor supplies the fourth case, more weakly. Its two spliced
forms are not equivalent as activators, and only the first induced a reporter
gene in a yeast assay [@slugina2021rinisoforms]. Whether a plant can make that
form depends on whether its RIN locus carries the relevant 3' splice site,
which several wild green-fruited species lack [@slugina2021rinisoforms].

An oilseed *Brassica rapa* line shows the same kind of allele skipping
vernalisation altogether. A 56 bp deletion at the fourth exon-intron boundary
of BrFLC2 introduces a premature stop and truncates the protein by 68 residues
[@kim2022brflc2]. Blocking translation-dependent decay with cycloheximide
restored the transcript, which places the loss of the repressor in
nonsense-mediated decay rather than in reduced transcription [@kim2022brflc2].
Both of those results were read from the preprint rather than from the
published version.

### Stress splicing is measured more often than it is explained

Stress changes plant splicing, and the literature on it is overwhelmingly
descriptive. An Arabidopsis experiment found 49.4 per cent of its
intron-containing genes alternatively spliced under salt, pooled across three
salt concentrations, and reported that a tenth of them shifted their isoform
ratio significantly with the stress [@ding2014salt]. Two cautions attach to
that figure, and neither is in the abstract. It has no companion measurement
in untreated plants, so it cannot be read as an increase, and the control
enters only as event counts, which were lower [@ding2014salt]. The depth
usually quoted for the study is also not the depth at which its splicing was
counted. The authors drew 18 million read pairs at random from each library
first, so that every condition was measured alike [@ding2014salt]. Maize grown
through realistic daily temperature cycles raised its splicing frequency as
maximum daily temperature rose. Retained introns and skipped exons increased
most. The splicing regulators were themselves among the genes most often
affected, SR45a among them [@li2021maize]. Light changes splicing in
Arabidopsis roots without being sensed there, since the signal traces to
sugars made by photosynthesis in the shoot acting through the TOR kinase
pathway [@riegler2021light].

What that body of work mostly lacks is a named gene whose isoform ratio was
perturbed on purpose, and the nearest case stops at biochemistry. Cold-induced
splicing of the rice cyclophilin gene OsCYP19-4 yields eight transcripts and
four proteins. Two of them are directed to guard and subsidiary cells rather
than the general epidermis, and one is sent to the endoplasmic reticulum
[@lee2016oscyp194]. The recombinant form with altered active-site residues had
significantly lower isomerase activity than the main form [@lee2016oscyp194].
Nobody has yet supplied one of those isoforms on its own and scored a plant
for cold tolerance. Against the flowering-time and immunity literature, where
isoform-restricted alleles are routine, the abiotic stress literature is a
collection of prevalence measurements. That gap is worth stating, because a
reader scanning review articles would not guess it.

## Fungi {#sec-fungi}

### Budding yeast is the exception that taught everyone the rule

Splicing is required in only about 4 per cent of *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*
protein-coding genes, and the genes that carry an intron are structurally
plain, typically two exons and one intron [@schreiber2015yeast]. The organism
that taught most biologists what splicing is makes a poor guide to what
splicing does. Within that small intron set, alternative splice site use is
not rare. A reanalysis found that most trustworthy junctions were already
annotated. Of the 170 that were not, 71 were alternative splice sites at known
introns and 99 were introns nobody had annotated [@schreiber2015yeast].

Some of that simplicity was acquired rather than ancestral. The widely
conserved alternatively spliced gene SKI7/HBS1 was replaced in *Saccharomyces*
by a pair of duplicated, intronless genes during whole-genome doubling, which
converted one isoform choice into two separate loci [@hurtig2020budding]. A
relative that kept the single gene shows what was lost. In *Lachancea
kluyveri* one SKI7/HBS1 gene produces two isoforms, and expressed in budding
yeast, one repairs an *hbs1* mutant but not a *ski7* mutant while the other
does the reverse [@marshall2013subfunctionalization]. Gene duplication and
alternative splicing reach the same destination.

### A yeast that keeps introns it almost never uses

If so few yeast genes need splicing, the introns that remain need an
explanation. Two papers published together in 2019 gave one, and both looked
past the protein. When every known intron was deleted one at a time, most of
the resulting strains grew worse than wild type once nutrients ran out
[@introns2019starvationmediators]. The effect survived blocking translation of
the gene the intron sat in, so the mechanism proposed is an indirect one
[@introns2019starvationmediators]. Introns help cells survive starvation by
deepening the shutdown of ribosomal protein genes downstream of the two
nutrient-sensing pathways [@introns2019starvationmediators]. That makes an
intron a lever on the splicing machinery's workload rather than a coding
element.

The companion paper gave the excised intron itself a job. Thirty-four introns
that are rapidly degraded during log-phase growth instead accumulate as linear
RNA when the growth-signalling kinase is inhibited. Deleting them hurts cells
in saturated culture and makes them grow abnormally fast under chronic
rapamycin. Putting a native or an engineered stable intron back suppresses
that [@introns2019excisedlinear]. What marks out the introns that survive
excision is structural rather than a sequence motif. They keep an unusually
short distance between the branch point and the 3' splice site, and they stay
bound to spliceosome components after release. That short distance is both
necessary and sufficient for persistence [@introns2019excisedlinear].

Six years later the same laboratory moved the explanation to the spliceosome's
own composition. U1 rises relative to the rest, binds a particular set of
introns more tightly, and splices them better. Only the introns spliced better
under starvation are the ones cells need to survive it
[@parenteau2025spliceswitch]. That is a narrower claim than "most introns",
and it comes from the group with most to lose by narrowing it.

Two further yeast introns matter for reasons of their own. Deleting a
predicted RNA structure from inside the GLC7 intron, leaving the intron in
place, removed the cell's ability to respond to salt stress, and the structure
acted only when present on the same molecule [@hooks2016intronicrna]. An
intron in the untranslated leader of the small ribosomal subunit gene RPS22B
splits a clonal population in two under osmotic stress, making protein levels
bimodal [@lukacisin2022intronheterogeneity]. The two subpopulations then trade
against each other. Low-protein cells outlast sustained starvation, while
high-protein cells recover faster from a brief one
[@lukacisin2022intronheterogeneity]. The YRA1 gene regulates itself through
its intron rather than through two proteins, using multiple elements inside it
to hold the unspliced message in a state that is both poorly translated and
selectively degraded [@dong2010yra1].

### Two loci where the choice has a consequence

How thin the ground was can be stated exactly. As of 2013, PTC7 was the only
budding yeast gene known to make two functional messages by splicing, and for
the gene now called HEH1 only the longer isoform had been shown to do anything
[@marshall2013subfunctionalization]. At PTC7, retaining or removing a single
intron sends the same phosphatase to two places, because the retained intron
encodes a membrane-spanning helix. The spliced message makes a mitochondrial
protein, and the intron-retained message makes one that sits in the nuclear
envelope [@marshall2013subfunctionalization]. The functional evidence behind
that clean localisation story is weak, and the same authors say so. Removing
either PTC7 isoform produces no phenotype a laboratory can easily see
[@marshall2013subfunctionalization].

HEH1 has since been worked out in more detail, and it is the better case.
Yeast chooses between two 5' splice sites four nucleotides apart, and the
choice changes the protein's far end [@banyal2025heh1]. The two products share
a front end, diverge at the back, and sit in the inner nuclear membrane in
different orientations [@banyal2025heh1]. That choice is also made unusually
late. A sixteen-nucleotide stretch spanning both candidate sites is read out
by two of the spliceosome's own RNAs, during the transition between assembly
intermediates [@banyal2025heh1]. The decision is taken inside the spliceosome
rather than by a dedicated regulatory protein. The short isoform also has a
job, visible once a second pathway is broken. In cells lacking an ESCRT-III
component, removing the short isoform as well causes severe growth defects and
a build-up of improperly assembled nuclear pores [@capella2020heh1]. Removing
the splicing factor that makes that isoform does the same [@capella2020heh1].
Only the long isoform carries the domain that recruits the membrane-scission
machinery, and the short isoform keeps that recruitment in check
[@capella2020heh1].
### Meiosis, and a spliceosome in short supply

What regulated splicing budding yeast retains is concentrated in meiosis. The
activator Mer1 is required to splice four meiosis-specific pre-mRNAs, MER2,
MER3, AMA1 and SPO22, whose introns are otherwise poor spliceosome substrates
[@venkataramanan2017meiotic]. Why those genes are the ones that benefit is a
question about supply. Their branch points and 5' splice sites are less well
conserved than the yeast average, so they get spliced only when the machinery is
not busy elsewhere [@venkataramanan2017meiotic].

That competition for the machinery is measurable. The spliceosome is in short
supply, so the cell's global splicing efficiency rises when the ribosomal
protein genes that consume most of it are switched off, and falls again when
they return [@premrna2013splicingcompetition]. That claim rests on a genetic
test rather than a correlation. Turning down the single transcription factor
driving the ribosomal protein genes rescued two separate spliceosome mutants.
It restored genome-wide splicing efficiency in one of them
[@premrna2013splicingcompetition]. Chromatin state feeds into the same circuit
from another direction. Deleting the remodelling ATPase Snf2 improved splicing
for most budding yeast introns, with the biggest gains at introns having
non-consensus signals [@venkataramanan2017meiotic]. Losing Snf2 shuts down the
ribosomal protein genes and frees the spliceosome.

Fission yeast runs comparable logic with the sign reversed, and the mechanism
there has been relocated rather than confirmed. The RNA-binding protein Mmi1
binds primary transcripts of thirty or more meiotic genes in vegetative cells.
It inhibits splicing of the introns lying near its binding sites while sparing
distant ones, and routes the transcript to hyperadenylation-dependent decay
[@chen2011mmi1]. At least 29 target genes are therefore transcribed
constitutively and expressed only in meiosis [@chen2011mmi1]. A second group
then found Mmi1 holding meiotic messages in nuclear foci, keeping them away
from the translation machinery. Its self-association through a partner protein
was required for the foci. The same was true for the degradation, the nuclear
retention and the block on protein output [@shichino2018mmi1foci]. On that
account the splicing inhibition is not the primary mechanism, and a chapter
should not assert it on one 2011 reading. One named locus does show the
splicing step being withheld. The meiotic cyclin gene *crs1* is transcribed
continuously in growing cells, while its transcripts are destroyed instead of
spliced and polyadenylated. In a mutant lacking Mmi1 those same vegetative
transcripts do get spliced and polyadenylated [@mcpheeters2009crs1].

### A fungal clock set by which start codon is used

The best functional isoform pair in the fungi belongs to a clock. In
*Neurospora crassa* the gene *frequency* is transcribed from two promoters
into at least six major mRNAs. The temperature sensitivity of one splicing
choice decides which initiation codon is used [@frq2005temperaturesplicing].
So the relative amounts of the two FREQUENCY proteins are set by splicing
rather than by transcription [@frq2005temperaturesplicing]. Strains engineered
to make only the long protein or only the short one both keep a running clock,
at different speeds: the long-only strain runs short and the short-only strain
runs long [@frq2007longshortisoforms].

That experiment also argues against the function the pair was assumed to serve.
Having both proteins is not what keeps the period stable across temperatures,
because each single-isoform strain is already temperature-compensated, and the
ratio instead trims period length to the ambient temperature
[@frq2007longshortisoforms]. A chapter that called this pair a temperature
compensation device would be contradicted by its own primary source.

The two proteins are not interchangeable biochemically either. The long form
carries an extra 99 residues at its front end, and is the less stable of the
two, turning over faster [@chen2023frqisoforms]. The short form binds more of
the White Collar activator complex that FREQUENCY exists to repress
[@chen2023frqisoforms]. That front-end segment is not decorative either.
Internal deletions inside its last thirty residues leave the fungus arrhythmic
in a race-tube assay [@chen2023frqisoforms]. Deletions elsewhere in the same
segment only shift the period [@chen2023frqisoforms]. A requirement that
specific falls on sequence that only one of the two isoforms contains. A
preprint adds that the segment is intrinsically disordered, and that altering
one motif inside it disrupts timekeeping only at particular temperatures. The
two isoforms also pull down different sets of interacting proteins
[@pelham2026proteoform].

### The intron-richest fungus does not diversify its proteins

Across the kingdom the splicing rate is higher than yeast suggests. A
comparative study of 23 fungi with sampling-depth correction estimated that
6.4 per cent of annotated fungal genes are alternatively spliced on average,
with *Cryptococcus neoformans* reaching 18 per cent [@grutzmann2013fungal].
Basidiomycota averaged 8.6 per cent against 6.0 per cent for Ascomycota, a
difference those authors call not significant [@grutzmann2013fungal]. Within
that dataset the rate rises with structural complexity. It runs from 0.26 per
cent in the mostly single-celled Saccharomycotina and Taphrinomycotina,
through 2.3 per cent in Mucoromycotina and 7.2 per cent in the filamentous
Pezizomycotina, to 8.6 per cent in the fruiting-body-forming Basidiomycota
[@grutzmann2013fungal].

![Within one comparative study using one method, per-gene alternative splicing
rate tracks how multicellular the group is. Rates from different studies cannot
be placed on an axis like this one.](../figures/fungal-as-ladder.svg){#fig-fungal-ladder width=100%}

A mushroom-forming fungus at the top of that ladder does use splicing broadly.
In *Schizophyllum commune*, 2,285 of 12,988 expressed genes produced more than
one transcript. That yields 15,522 transcripts in all, about a fifth more
transcripts than genes [@gehrmann2016schizophyllum]. Most of the alternative
transcripts would change the protein. Some 69 per cent of the spliced genes
gain or lose a functional domain, or acquire a different predicted location
[@gehrmann2016schizophyllum]. Those consequences are computational predictions
rather than measurements, and that figure should be read as one.

The intron content of fungi spans about fortyfold, which makes "fungal" a poor
unit. The range runs from 2.4 per cent of genes carrying introns in *Candida
glabrata* to more than 99 per cent in *Cryptococcus neoformans*, with 14.5 per
cent in *Yarrowia lipolytica* and 47 per cent in fission yeast in between
[@gonzalezhilarion2016cryptococcusir]. Fission yeast is the intermediate case
the ladder needs. About 43 per cent of its genes carry introns, often more
than one, which is why it can be used to study splicing at all
[@montanes2022fissionyeast]. It now has a direct figure as well. Reading
native RNA molecules end to end found 332 alternative isoforms that change the
coding sequence of 262 genes. Of those, 97 were present at more than a fifth
of the gene's output [@montanes2022fissionyeast]. The older number for the
same species is weaker than its circulation suggests. The fungal survey's
introduction places fission yeast in a nought-to-five per cent band with
budding yeast and two other species, and attributes the whole band to one
earlier comparative study [@grutzmann2013fungal].

*Cryptococcus* is intron-rich by any measure, carrying 40,946 introns, with
99.5 per cent of its expressed genes containing at least one
[@janbon2014cryptococcus]. The obvious inference from that is wrong.
Re-annotating the organism and comparing conditions confirmed that nearly
every expressed gene is alternatively spliced, and that environmental cues
regulate it. Those same authors conclude that alternative splicing is an
inefficient way to vary this organism's proteome
[@gonzalezhilarion2016cryptococcusir]. What the retained introns do instead is
set expression level, by a route that does not run through nonsense-mediated
decay [@gonzalezhilarion2016cryptococcusir]. That implies the unspliced
message is held in the nucleus rather than destroyed in the cytoplasm. The
positional evidence fits the same reading. More than 99 per cent of coding
introns sit at identical positions in the two varieties compared.
Untranslated-region introns are far less conserved, least of all at the 3' end
[@gonzalezhilarion2016cryptococcusir]. One gene has been followed through the
mechanism. It is transcribed equally at 30 and 37 degrees but spliced poorly
at the lower temperature, so its protein output is set by how much of its
intron is removed [@gonzalezhilarion2016cryptococcusir].

### Infection, symbiosis and a scalpel rather than a programme

Pathogens remodel their isoform repertoire as they invade. Transcriptome data
from the rice blast fungus *Magnaporthe oryzae* spanned vegetative growth and
five stages of rice infection. It yielded 4,270 novel mRNA isoforms from 2,413
genes, 18.1 per cent of the gene set [@jeon2022riceblast]. Two loci in that
fungus have been taken further. Its PTEN homologue is spliced two ways, and
the two products were separated and tested. The full gene restores every
defect of the deletion mutant [@wang2021mopten]. The intron-retained form only
partially restores spore and penetration-structure formation, and the spliced
form only partially restores growth inside the plant [@wang2021mopten]. Its
single phosphotransfer gene yields at least three transcripts whose levels
respond to different stresses, and the corresponding proteins enter the
nucleus under different stresses. Strains built to make only one of them are
each less virulent than wild type [@buhring2024moypd1]. The same group had
earlier made the transcript-level case for that locus and detected one
previously unknown protein isoform by mass spectrometry, which is what
justifies treating the later result as isoform-specific
[@buhring2021moypd1isoform].

Two human pathogens run the same arrangement at a stress-response gene, and
both show its limits. *Cryptococcus* handles unfolded proteins through a
transcription factor gene, HXL1, that is cut by the kinase Ire1 rather than by
the spliceosome. Supplying the already-spliced version of that gene repairs
every growth defect of a cell that has lost Ire1 [@cheon2011hxl1]. That puts
the splicing event at the functional step rather than the kinase. But the same
allele test marks the limit. Capsule synthesis is lost when Ire1 is deleted
and not when its target transcription factor is. Neither allele of the target
restores capsule, so one branch of the pathway runs without the splicing event
[@cheon2011hxl1]. Losing the kinase costs the fungus everything that matters.
Mice infected with the mutant were still healthy 42 days on, and mice given
wild type or the complemented strain fell ill between 18 and 23 days
[@cheon2011hxl1].

*Candida albicans* repeats the shape of that answer in a different species.
Its HAC1 message carries a 19-base-pair intron that Ire1 removes under
endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and no spliced message appears in cells whose
Ire1 is compromised. The Hac1-dependent target genes track the spliced message
rather than the total [@sircaik2021candidaire1]. The splicing event is
nevertheless not what drives the shape change that matters for infection. The
switch to filaments involves only limited HAC1 splicing compared with
proteotoxic stress. Deleting HAC1 impairs filamentation only partly, while
deleting the kinase above it abolishes filamentation almost entirely
[@stackcouture2026ire1morphogenesis]. In the same organism the amount of
intron retention rises when the yeast switches to its filamentous form, and
crippling the spliceosome pushes retention higher and blocks the switch
altogether [@lash2024candidaspliceosome]. That last perturbation is a
core-subunit deletion, so it implicates splicing in general rather than any
isoform.

Comparing pathogens tells against the idea of a conserved splicing programme.
Across seven human fungal pathogens under host-like and stress conditions, not
one of the genes with a condition-dependent isoform shift had a counterpart
doing the same thing in every other species examined [@sieber2018pathogens].
Isoform shifts and expression changes also pick out largely different genes,
overlapping for only about a seventh of them [@sieber2018pathogens]. That is
the argument for splicing as a separate control layer rather than a by-product
of transcription.

Some fungi operate the host's splicing machinery instead of their own.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi reach into their host to establish symbiosis. The
Glomeromycotina-specific SP7-like effector family collects in nuclear
condensates, and binds the plant splicing factor SR45 together with the core
spliceosome proteins U1-70K and U2AF35 [@betz2024mycorrhizal]. The grip on
that factor is narrow and has been mapped. The carboxy-terminal
arginine-serine domain of SR45 is both required and on its own sufficient for
the effector to bind it, while the RNA-binding motif and the other
arginine-serine domain are dispensable [@betz2024mycorrhizal]. The effect on
the host is narrower still, and this is the number worth keeping. Expressing
one of these effectors in potato left root gene expression broadly changed
while shifting the splicing of only 96 genes out of the 7,161 the crop is
predicted to splice alternatively [@betz2024mycorrhizal]. Selectivity, rather
than reach, is what that experiment demonstrates.
## Protists and parasites {#sec-protists}

Most of what follows is architecture and prevalence rather than function, and
two cases are the exception. It is worth saying at the outset that much of the
apicomplexan work in this chapter comes from one laboratory, which limits how
independent the agreement between those records is.

### A virulence phenotype with no identified mis-spliced target

Deleting the splicing factor SR2 from *Toxoplasma gondii* cut the brain cyst
burden in infected mice by about 80 per cent, from roughly 216 cysts per brain
in wild type to 46 in the knockout, and complementation restored the wild-type
level [@wu2023sr2]. That is a splicing regulator behaving as a virulence
determinant, and it is as far as the evidence goes. The same knockout
converted from tachyzoite to bradyzoite at wild-type rates at every alkaline
pH tested, so the defect does not reproduce in culture, and the paper reports
no sequencing of the mutant [@wu2023sr2]. No transcript has been identified as
the intermediary between losing the factor and losing the cysts.

The kinases above those factors are similarly unresolved. Where humans and
Arabidopsis each carry families of SRPK and CLK paralogues, phylogenetic
assignment recovers a single SRPK and a single CLK in both *Toxoplasma* and
*Plasmodium falciparum* [@lee2021tgsr]. Knocking down the two *Toxoplasma*
kinases that phosphorylate SR proteins killed the parasite and changed
splicing widely [@lee2021tgsr]. The transcripts they affected did not match
those affected by deleting the individual SR proteins, so a kinase and its
presumed substrates do not share a regulon [@lee2021tgsr]. That is a warning
about reasoning from regulator to target, and the work is a preprint.

A splicing factor can also run the other way. In *Entamoeba histolytica*,
deleting an unusual domain from EhU2AF2 increased splicing and increased
virulence, both in culture and in animals, which is the opposite direction to
the *Toxoplasma* result [@gonzalezblanco2022u2af2]. The sign of these effects is
not a property of splicing regulators in parasites.

### Deleting a retained intron restores a protein, and a flagellum

The strongest functional result in the parasites deletes an intron from the
genome. In the rodent malaria parasite *Plasmodium yoelii*, removing
*kinesin8b* intron 1 restored Kinesin8B protein to wild-type levels in
parasites lacking the splicing activator RBPm1 [@guan2024axonemal]. The same
trick worked for PF16 intron 1 and for one further gene, with partial
restoration at a fourth [@guan2024axonemal]. Structure came partly back along
with the protein. Male gametocytes lacking RBPm1 built no intact axonemes at
all, and removing *kinesin8b* intron 1 recovered a minority with recognisable
microtubule arrangements [@guan2024axonemal]. Removing PF16 intron 1 as well
gave a further gain [@guan2024axonemal]. That remains far short of the 93 per
cent of wild-type axonemes that are normal, which is what one would expect if
the programme has other members [@guan2024axonemal].

Splicing also separates the sexes in a related parasite. Ablating the
male-gametocyte SR protein PbSR-MG in *Plasmodium berghei* changed splicing in
about a tenth of male-gametocyte genes. The same ablation changed 3.9 per cent
of female genes and 0.90 per cent of asexual-stage genes
[@yeoh2019stagedifferentiation]. It altered the expression level of just 0.5
per cent of genes, which separates the splicing effect from a transcriptional
one [@yeoh2019stagedifferentiation]. The consequence of losing it is a failure
of transmission. Knockout male gametocytes almost never exflagellated where up
to 36 per cent of wild-type males did, and the few gametes released were close
to immotile [@yeoh2019stagedifferentiation]. Mosquito oocyst numbers fell even
when equal numbers of ookinetes were fed [@yeoh2019stagedifferentiation].
Supplying the full-length gene on an artificial chromosome reverted both
defects [@yeoh2019stagedifferentiation]. The gamete fusion factor HAP2 shifts
its own splicing as male gametocytes form, with relatively more transcripts
retaining a longer first intron than in blood stages, which is a correlation
rather than a test [@yeoh2019stagedifferentiation].

How much splicing these parasites do at all depends on what is counted.
*Plasmodium falciparum* is not the intron-poor organism it is often taken for,
since over half its genes carry predicted introns. Gene-model-independent
analysis of the blood stages added 977 previously undocumented canonical
splice junctions, an 11 per cent increase on the annotation
[@sorber2011plasmodium]. Direct long-read sequencing of native RNA put the
share of expressed genes carrying at least one retained intron at 70.22 per
cent in *Toxoplasma* and 44.33 per cent in *P. falciparum*
[@lee2021apicomplexan]. The proportions held when the analysis was restricted
to genes with ten or more reads [@lee2021apicomplexan]. Those figures are
retention over expressed genes in one experiment rather than an alternative
splicing rate. They should not be read beside the plant percentages earlier in
this chapter. Retention there is not a trickle at the edge of detection. In
more than half their transcripts, 808 *Toxoplasma* genes and 162 *P.
falciparum* genes keep a genuine annotated intron [@lee2021apicomplexan]. The
gap between the two species tracks intron number, since *Toxoplasma* averages
4.5 introns per gene against 1.5 in *Plasmodium* [@lee2021apicomplexan]. Most
of it is unlikely to be making protein. More than seven in ten
intron-retaining reads from either parasite terminate prematurely by the
55-nucleotide rule, which those authors read as a route to transcript turnover
[@lee2021apicomplexan]. *Toxoplasma* also shows what the method does to the
answer. Junction-level counting that deliberately ignores intron retention put
alternative splicing at 22.6 per cent of annotated genes in uninduced
parasites, against roughly 5 per cent from earlier studies built on
reconstructing transcript models [@yeoh2015toxoplasma]. The organism did not
change between those two numbers.

### Trypanosomes put the splice site where the gene boundary is

Trypanosomes rearranged the problem altogether, and did so long before anyone
could sequence a transcriptome. Their messenger RNAs were shown to share an
identical 35-nucleotide leader at the 5' end, present on many and probably all
of them [@parsons1984splicedleader]. Genes are transcribed polycistronically,
and individual mature mRNAs are carved out of that transcript by
spliced-leader trans-splicing, obligatorily coupled to cleavage and
polyadenylation in the intergenic regions [@kolev2026transsplicing]. The
splicing reaction there sets transcript boundaries instead of choosing
internal exon content.

That coupling was established by mutagenesis rather than inference. Blocks of
the intergenic region between the beta- and alpha-tubulin genes were replaced
one at a time. One pyrimidine-rich tract at the alpha-tubulin splice acceptor
determines both accurate trans-splicing downstream of itself and 3'-end
formation upstream [@pyrimidine1994transsplicing]. Destroying that tract
produced cryptic splice site use, and misplaced poly(A) sites even where the
wild-type poly(A) site was left intact [@pyrimidine1994transsplicing].

Choosing between acceptor sites is the trypanosome equivalent of choosing an
exon, and one gene shows the choice doing work. *Trypanosoma brucei* runs a
single isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase gene as two proteins by choosing where to add
the spliced leader. RNA interference aimed only at the 5' untranslated region
unique to the longer variant removed the mitochondrial protein and left the
cytosolic one untouched, after which uncharged isoleucine tRNA piled up inside
the mitochondrion while the cytosolic pool stayed charged
[@rettig2011dualtargeting]. The ratio between the two is set partly by decay
rather than by site choice alone. The cytosolic short variant is three to four
times the more abundant, and after transcription was blocked the long variant
fell to half its level in about 22 minutes against about 66 minutes for the
short one [@rettig2011dualtargeting].

Whether that mechanism broadens the proteome in general is a separate
question, and the genome-wide test says no. The internal start codons that
alternative acceptor sites would expose are no better conserved between *T.
brucei* and *T. cruzi* than other internal ATG codons
[@soulette2019transsplicing]. The genuine first codons of open reading frames
clearly are so conserved, and ribosome profiling did not show the alternative
ones occupied [@soulette2019transsplicing]. A stage-specific version of the
question gets a similar answer. *Leishmania major* does shift which
spliced-leader site it prefers as it becomes infective, with 523 of 8,797
genes changing their primary acceptor between the procyclic and metacyclic
stages [@dillon2015leishmania]. The genes that switched were no more likely to
change expression level than those that did not, so the switching does not
look like the mechanism of differentiation [@dillon2015leishmania].

### Regulation or error, argued over one ciliate

Ciliates run splicing close to its physical minimum. Every *Paramecium* intron
falls in a narrow 25 to 45 base pair range, among the shortest known anywhere.
Those authors read that as a functional limit for spliceosomal recognition
[@bondarenko2016ciliate]. The group differs internally in how much splicing it
does. Average introns per gene run 1.6 to 2.3 in *Paramecium* and *Oxytricha*
but 4.8 in *Tetrahymena* [@bondarenko2016ciliate]. The alveolate ancestor is
reconstructed as intron-rich, so the intron poverty is loss rather than
inheritance [@bondarenko2016ciliate]. Deep sequencing across growth,
starvation and conjugation put alternative splicing in *Tetrahymena* at 1,474
events over 1,286 genes, 5.2 per cent of the gene set [@xiong2012tetrahymena].
Intron retention was the largest class, and 172 of those genes were spliced
differently in only one life-cycle stage [@xiong2012tetrahymena].

What that retention means is disputed, in the same organism. On one reading it
is regulation with a safety net. *Paramecium*'s tiny introns are under
selection to put a stop codon in frame if they are left in
[@translational2008intronsplicing]. Knocking down both UPF1 genes showed that
the decay pathway removes a substantial part of the unspliced fraction
[@translational2008intronsplicing]. On the other reading it is error. A test
built on the premise that mis-splicing costs more in highly expressed and
intron-rich genes concluded that 92 to 98 per cent of the splice variants seen
at median expression in *Paramecium* are mistakes [@saudemont2017missplicing].
That pattern held in cells with the decay pathway disabled, which is what
makes it hard to answer, since a regulatory interpretation would predict the
relationship to depend on decay [@saudemont2017missplicing]. No functional
isoform case has been established in any ciliate in this corpus, which is
itself worth recording.

### An oomycete effector that keeps its intron

One case outside the animals, plants and fungi meets the standard of the best
plant examples. An oomycete turns a transporter gene into a secreted effector
by leaving an intron in. When intron 1 of the *Pseudoperonospora cubensis*
gene Psc_781.4 is retained, a stop codon comes into frame. The transcript then
encodes a 132-amino-acid protein that keeps a signal peptide and an RXLR
motif, while losing the EamA transporter domain that its 332-residue
*Phytophthora infestans* orthologue retains [@savory2012oomycete]. The two
isoforms differ in what they do to a plant. Expressing the intron-retained
short form in *Nicotiana benthamiana* produced chlorosis across the whole
infiltration zone within two days, and dead tissue by seven
[@savory2012oomycete]. The fully spliced long form of the same gene produced
no cell death at all, and neither did the *Phytophthora* orthologue
[@savory2012oomycete].

### The supergroups with nothing to report

Several eukaryotic supergroups have no isoform case at all, and the honest
account of them is a count of introns. Amoebozoa is the clearest example of
that emptiness. One comparison counted 441 exact intron losses in
*Dictyostelium discoideum* and 202 in *D. purpureum* [@ma2015dictyostelium].
The lost introns sat further from the 5' end of genes than the retained ones,
and the higher-loss species carried significantly more reverse transcriptase
genes [@ma2015dictyostelium]. Those authors read that as loss through gene
conversion with reverse-transcribed cDNA, which is a model rather than a
demonstration [@ma2015dictyostelium].

*Giardia intestinalis* has almost no cis-spliced introns to splice
alternatively. Strand-specific sequencing of four isolates confirmed the
handful already known and added exactly one new intron, 36 nucleotides long
[@franzen2013giardia]. PCR testing rejected 13 of the 14 further candidates
that junction mapping had proposed [@franzen2013giardia]. *Trichomonas
vaginalis* is likewise close to intronless, and its count has kept moving. A
chromosome-scale assembly with deep transcriptome support settled on 63 active
introns plus 34 apparently inactive intron sequences
[@callejas2025trichomonas]. The same count was 41 in 2005 and 32 in 2018, and
one active intron is 23 nucleotides long [@callejas2025trichomonas].

Two lineages have more to work with. The model diatom *Phaeodactylum
tricornutum* carries 8,646 introns, 0.7 per gene, with about 53 per cent of
its genes predicted to carry none at all [@rastogi2018phaeodactylum]. Across
seventeen growth and stress conditions, 2,924 of its 12,177 gene models showed
intron retention and 2,444 showed exon skipping, with 1,335 showing both
[@rastogi2018phaeodactylum]. Retention leads skipping there as it does in
other single-celled eukaryotes. Under nitrogen starvation the genes retaining
introns rose in expression while those skipping exons fell, which runs
opposite to the negative relationship between retention and expression
reported in the apicomplexans and in *Paramecium* [@rastogi2018phaeodactylum].
Red algae mostly dismantled their splicing machinery as their genomes shrank,
and *Galdieria* is the exception. Of 155 spliceosome-associated genes inferred
for the red algal common ancestor it retains 150, against 53 to 145 across the
other lineages examined [@qiu2018galdieria]. It carries about two introns per
gene where others have under 0.34, and some of those introns are spliced
differently at different culture temperatures [@qiu2018galdieria].

## Whether any of this tracks complexity {#sec-trend}

*Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* split from land plants around a billion years ago,
and gives the green lineage a baseline. It shows alternative splicing at 498
transcriptional units and 611 events, about 3 per cent of its gene count
[@labadorf2010chlamydomonas]. It sits in the gap the plant lineage had to
cross, far below land plants and clearly above simple unicellular heterotrophs
[@labadorf2010chlamydomonas]. Its mix of event classes already resembles that
of flowering plants [@labadorf2010chlamydomonas].

The coverage-corrected index of eukaryotic splicing was built from more than
39 million ESTs downloaded for 112 species, of which 47 passed a filter
requiring 500 genes with comparable estimates [@chen2014complexity]. Across
those 47 the index rose steadily over roughly 1,400 million years of
eukaryotic evolution, with plants scoring higher than both fungi and protists
[@chen2014complexity]. Those authors read that as an independent increase in
the plant lineage rather than a shared trend [@chen2014complexity]. The
attrition from 112 to 47 is worth knowing before leaning on that conclusion.
The species that started were 20 protists, 18 plants, 23 fungi and 51
metazoans, and the survivors were six protists, ten plants, six fungi and
twenty-five metazoans [@chen2014complexity]. The finding that plants
out-splice the microbial eukaryotes therefore rests on ten plant genomes
against twelve others.

The complexity correlation in the same study weakens substantially under its
own authors' correction. Regressing out how many transcripts each species had
sequenced, the variance in cell type number explained by events per gene falls
from 0.83 to 0.47 [@chen2014complexity]. The variance explained by proportion
of genes spliced falls from 0.76 to 0.57, while the ranking of predictors is
unchanged [@chen2014complexity]. The vertebrate-over-invertebrate difference
survives the same kind of objection. A method built not to depend on how many
ESTs each organism had was applied to the same eight species. It still put
both the percentage of genes and the percentage of exons spliced alternatively
higher in vertebrates [@kim2006eukaryotes].

### One organism, two numbers, one method

Re-measuring old species with one uniform method does not merely tidy a
ranking. The fungal survey's own random-sampling estimate for *Cryptococcus
neoformans* is 18.2 and 19.9 per cent of genes for its two sequenced strains,
against the 4.2 per cent its own introduction cites from a single-species
study of the same fungus [@grutzmann2013fungal]. The gap is fourfold and sits
inside one paper. Both strains drew on the same EST data, so this is one
dataset measured two ways [@grutzmann2013fungal]. *Cryptococcus* is also well
sampled, so sparse data cannot explain the gap [@grutzmann2013fungal]. Why the
uniform method reproduces the two yeasts and overturns this fungus is not
stated.

### The comparisons that survive

Two things are being measured in all of this, and they move separately. How much
alternative splicing a lineage does is one quantity. Which classes of event it
uses is another, and the switch from cassette exons to intron retention happens
without regard to the first.

The reassuring result is that rankings outlive their numbers. Two studies that
applied the same ten-transcript normalisation got different absolute
percentages and the same ordering [@chen2014complexity]. The later and larger
survey reported higher proportions for most clades, while the differences
between clades agreed [@chen2014complexity]. Four studies spanning three
generations of sequencing found the same confounder pointing the same way.
Each time the absolute values moved while the order held.

The figures in this chapter are therefore measurements of experiments that
happen to be about organisms. Any single number offered for an organism is a
property of the assay as much as of the organism. The comparisons that survive
are the ones made inside a single study, and the claims that survive best are
the ones where somebody changed which isoform an organism could make and then
watched what it did.
